newsitem.title: GREECE: Princess Diana joins in funeral on Greek island.
newsitem.headline: Princess Diana joins in funeral on Greek island.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana on Wednesday attended the Orthodox funeral of a young Greek she met during one of her mercy visits to a London hospital.

"God sent her to you at a difficult time to give you courage with her frequent visits," the local priest, Father Pavlos, said at the funeral service in this mining and tourist town on the Greek island of Evia.
Dressed in black and wearing a necklace of white pearls, she arrived by car in the picturesque coastal town on Evia, which is northeast of Athens and linked to the mainland by a bridge.
Diana quietly joined local mourners attending the funeral of Yannis Kalyviotis, 27, who died in London at the weekend of cystic fibrosis, a non-contagious, hereditary disease.

Turning to Diana, Father Pavlos said: "May the Lord give peace and happiness to your heart and help you in your work." Then turning to the others, he said: "Her presence here now is a lesson in love and humility."
Diana met Kalyviotis on one of her regular visits to London hospitals about 18 months ago and his struggle had touched the Princess's heart, friends of the family told Reuters.
Diana, who divorced the heir to the British throne, Prince Charles, in August, sat with Kalyviotis' mother at her home in Limni before going to the service at the nearby church.
"She met him 18 months ago in a London hospital and visited him often," said Voula Emmanouel, a friend of the family.
Kalyviotis, whom Emmanouel described as "intelligent, kind and educated", finished Athens law school while struggling with his long-term illness.
Diana visited his family's modest home as cousins hugged and wept outside. His widowed mother wailed from inside her home, crying out "My Yannis. My Yannis."
"If Diana has come as a mother and a fellow human being, she is welcome. I have the impression she is here for humanitarian reason," said neighbour Costas Costopoulos.
Friends in this town of 2,500 said many had been touched by the tragedy of the Kalyviotis family and his mother's fight to help her son by taking him to hospitals in the United States and Britain.
"They were loved and respected by the whole community and have everybody's support," said Costopoulos.
Several tourists were surprised to see Princess Diana arrive suddenly in this little-known village.
"I think it's a lovely gesture. I don't think she's a publicity seeker. She's a lovely person," said Mark Tyson, who lives in London.
Irishman Tom Moore, from Dublin, had a more jaundiced view: "If the British taxpayer is happy, it's fine by me."
Diana made no comment to reporters when she arrived in Athens earlier and kept her head bowed most of the time, avoiding a direct look into television cameras.
She also avoided reporters who trailed her to Limni but Greek media helicopters circled overhead to get pictures of her walking to the local church.
Diana was not expected to stay long in Greece. She is due at a gala dinner in Washington next Tuesday.
